q-166602.name: Question 1
q-166602.problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{-3}$ can be used to transform the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={y}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-y\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $P(x)?$
q-166602.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{-3}\,⟹\,y={z}^{-1/3}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-3{y}^{-4}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{3{z}^{4/3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3{z}^{4/3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{z}^{4/3}}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\frac{1}{{z}^{1/3}}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

We now write the above equation in standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x).
$$

In doing so, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3z\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-3z\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $P(x)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$

Question 1
?

The substitution z=y−3 can be used to transform the equation dydx=y4cos⁡x−ysin⁡x into an equation of the form z′(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x). What is the function P(x)?

a
−xcos⁡x
b
−3sin⁡x
c
3cos⁡x
d
tan⁡x
e
x2sin⁡x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we make the substitution z=y−3⟹y=z−1/3. Differentiating z(x) using the chain rule, we get dzdx=−3y−4dydx⟹dydx=−13z4/3dzdx.

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of z as follows: −13z4/3dzdx=1z4/3cos⁡x−1z1/3sin⁡x

We now write the above equation in standard form dzdx+P(x)z=Q(x).

In doing so, we obtain dzdx=−3cos⁡x+3zsin⁡xdzdx−3zsin⁡x=−3cos⁡x.

Therefore, P(x)=−3sin⁡x.

q-79781.name: Question 2
q-79781.problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{-2}$ can be used to transform the equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}y(1-x{y}^{2})
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $Q(x)?$
q-79781.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{-2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-2{y}^{-3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{2}{z}^{-3/2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}{z}^{-3/2}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{z}^{-1/2}(1-x{z}^{-1}) \\ {z}^{-3/2}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{2}{z}^{-1/2}(x{z}^{-1}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

We now write the above equation in standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x).
$$

In doing so, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{2}z(x{z}^{-1}-1) \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{3}-{x}^{2}z \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+{x}^{2}z & ={x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $Q(x)={x}^{3}.$

Question 2
?

The substitution z=y−2 can be used to transform the equation dydx=12x2y(1−xy2) into an equation of the form z′(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x). What is the function Q(x)?

a
x3
b
x
c
x2
d
1
e
1x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we make the substitution z=y−2. Differentiating z(x) using the chain rule, we get dzdx=−2y−3dydx⟹dydx=−12z−3/2dzdx.

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of z as follows: −12z−3/2dzdx=12x2z−1/2(1−xz−1)z−3/2dzdx=x2z−1/2(xz−1−1)

We now write the above equation in standard form dzdx+P(x)z=Q(x).

In doing so, we obtain dzdx=x2z(xz−1−1)dzdx=x3−x2zdzdx+x2z=x3.

Therefore, Q(x)=x3.

q-17554.name: Question 3
q-17554.problem:
Find the general solution to the following equation.

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{y(y-1)}{x}=0
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the substitution* $z={y}^{-1}.$
q-17554.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{-1}\,⟹\,y={z}^{-1}\,
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ with the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{{z}^{-1}({z}^{-1}-1)}{x} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{z({z}^{-1}-1)}{x} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1-z}{x} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1-z}{x} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x}+\frac{z}{x} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z & =\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{1}{x},\,Q(x)=\frac{1}{x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=x$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (\frac{dz}{dx}+\frac{1}{x}z) & =x\cdot (\frac{1}{x}) \\ x\frac{dz}{dx}+z & =1 \\ \frac{d}{dx}(zx) & =1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dx}(zx)\,dx & =\int 1\,dx \\ zx & =x+C \\ z & =\frac{x+C}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1} & =\frac{x+C}{x} \\ y & =\frac{x}{x+C}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Find the general solution to the following equation. dydx+y(y−1)x=0

Hint: You may wish to make use of the substitution z=y−1.

a
y=xx+C
b
y=−1x+C
c
y=x−1+Cx
d
y=x1+Cx
e
y=x1+Cex
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we make the substitution z=y−1⟹y=z−1

Differentiating z(x) with the chain rule, we get dzdx=−1y2dydx⟹dydx=−1z2dzdx.

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of z as follows: −1z2dzdx+z−1(z−1−1)x=0dzdx−z(z−1−1)x=0dzdx−1−zx=0

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form: dzdx−1−zx=0dzdx−1x+zx=0dzdx+1xz=1x

The above equation is in the standard form dzdx+P(x)z=Q(x) with P(x)=1x,Q(x)=1x.

We then compute an integrating factor: I(x)=e∫P(x)dx=e∫(1/x)dx=eln⁡x=x

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by I(x)=x yields x⋅(dzdx+1xz)=x⋅(1x)xdzdx+z=1ddx(zx)=1.

Now, we integrate with respect to x: ∫ddx(zx)dx=∫1dxzx=x+Cz=x+Cx

Finally, we determine y(x) by writing z=y−1. This results in y−1=x+Cxy=xx+C.

q-168136.problem:
Find the general solution to the following equation. 

$$
x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}-y\,,\,x>0
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the substitution $z={y}^{3}.$*
q-168136.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{3}\,⟹\,y={z}^{1/3}\,.
$$

Differentiating $y(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3{z}^{2/3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(\frac{1}{3{z}^{2/3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}) & =\frac{1}{{z}^{2/3}}-{z}^{1/3} \\ \frac{x}{3{z}^{2/3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{z}^{2/3}}-{z}^{1/3}\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{3{z}^{2/3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{z}^{2/3}}-{z}^{1/3} \\ \frac{x}{3}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1-z \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3}{x}\,z & =\frac{3}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
P(x)=\frac{3}{x},\,Q(x)=\frac{3}{x}\,.
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)dx} \\  & ={e}^{\int 3/xdx} \\  & ={e}^{3\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{3}} \\  & ={x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Under the condition that $x>0.$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)={x}^{3}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3}{x}\,z) & ={x}^{3}\cdot \frac{3}{x} \\ {x}^{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+3{x}^{2}z & =3{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[{x}^{3}z] & =3{x}^{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[{x}^{3}z]\,\text{d}x & =\int 3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ {x}^{3}z & ={x}^{3}+C \\ z & =1+\frac{C}{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{3}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{3} & =1+\frac{C}{{x}^{3}} \\ y & =\sqrt[3]{1+\frac{C}{{x}^{3}}},\end{aligned}
$$

q-79851.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{4}{x}y=-6{x}^{2}{y}^{3/2},\,y(1)=\frac{1}{9},\,y>0.
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the fact that the given differential equation can be transformed into the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{2}{x}\,z=3{x}^{2}
$$

using the substitution $z={y}^{-1/2}.$*
q-79851.worked_solution:
The substitution $z={y}^{-1/2}$ transforms the given equation into the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{2}{x}\,z=3{x}^{2},
$$

with the initial condition

$$
z(1)={(\frac{1}{9})}^{-1/2}=3\,.
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
P(x)=-\frac{2}{x},\,Q(x)=3{x}^{2}\,.
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-2\int 1/x\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{-2}} \\  & ={x}^{-2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)={x}^{-2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{2}{x}\,z) & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\cdot 3{x}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}\,z & =3 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,z) & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,z)\,\text{d}x & =\int 3\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,z & =3x+C \\ z & =3{x}^{3}+C{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we determine the value of $C$ that satisfies the initial condition $z(1)=3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z(1) & =3 \\ 3(1)^{3}+C(1)^{2} & =3 \\ 3+C & =3 \\ C & =0\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have 

$$
z=3{x}^{3}\,.
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by substituting the solution into $z={y}^{-1/2}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1/2} & =z \\ {y}^{-1/2} & =3{x}^{3} \\ {y}^{1/2} & =\frac{1}{3{x}^{3}} \\ y & =\frac{1}{9{x}^{6}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Solve the initial value problem dydx+4xy=−6x2y3/2,y(1)=19,y>0.

Hint: You may wish to make use of the fact that the given differential equation can be transformed into the equation dzdx−2xz=3x2 using the substitution z=y−1/2.

a
y=1(x3+2)2
b
y=34x6
c
y=4(5x3+x2)2
d
y=1(2x3+x2)2
e
y=19x6
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The substitution z=y−1/2 transforms the given equation into the equation dzdx−2xz=3x2,

with the initial condition z(1)=(19)−1/2=3.

The above equation is in the standard form dzdx+P(x)z=Q(x)

with P(x)=−2x,Q(x)=3x2.

q-168139.problem:
Solve the initial value problem 

$$
{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{y}^{2}=xy,\,y(1)=\frac{1}{3},\,x>0.
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the fact that the given differential equation can be transformed into the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}
$$

using the substitution $z={y}^{-1}.$*
q-168139.worked_solution:
The substitution $z={y}^{-1}$ transforms the given equation into the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{1}{x},\,Q(x)=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|} \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

under the condition that $x>0.$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=x$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z) & =x\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ x\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z & =\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz) & =\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ xz & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+C \\ z & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x+C}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1} & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x+C}{x} \\ y & =\frac{x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x+C}\end{aligned}
$$

We now determine $C$ from the initial condition  $y(1)=\frac{1}{3}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡1+C} \\ \frac{1}{3} & =\frac{1}{0+C} \\ C & =3\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x+3}.\end{aligned}
$$
